Uncertainty remains regarding whether a smaller, more recent incident in 2023-2024 has been misattributed or if the 23-death figure was updated in sources not yet archived. **Concrete Test** 1. This discrepancy could stem from: - **Conflation with broader regional data:** Tanzania’s Morogoro Region has multiple documented accidents (e.g., the 2016 earthquake with 11 deaths, the 2019 fuel tanker blast with 61 deaths). The "23 deaths" figure may refer to a separate incident (e.g., a 2022 collision in a different sub-location) that was later misattributed to Mkambarani. - **Unreviewed local sources:** The Archive’s "unreviewed" status for all findings implies no cross-validation with Tanzanian government or police reports (e.g., the 2023–2024 collision’s official toll may exist in Swahili-language sources not yet ingested). **Uncertainty:** The proposed test (Echo’s 1–3) assumes: - **Query completeness:** That "Mkambarani" is the only possible variant of the location name, ignoring administrative boundary shifts (e.g., Mkambarani may have been reclassified post-2020). - **Date specificity:** That the 28-death claim refers to a single event, whereas Tanzanian accident reports often aggregate fatalities over weeks (e.g., a series of truck collisions in 2023 may have been conflated into one figure). - **Source reliability:** That local outlets like *The Citizen* or *Daily News* would report a 28-death toll without cross-checking with police (e.g., Liberatus Sabas’ 23-death statement may have been updated or corrected in later editions). **Missing Control:** The proposal does not account for **temporal granularity in verified findings.** The "23 deaths" claim (Aljazeera, 2016) predates the frontier questions (2023–2024).
